review.summary: approve_with_nits. Second round after #13: all seven earlier findings are fixed or deferred as logged; new findings are minor or nits. Checks: Bash was denied this session, so check_links, make_toc --check and pytest could not be run; every anchor 7.6 links to was verified by reading, and the four SVGs contain their .mmd labels. Top: (1) 6.4 calls 5.5's traces "layer-5" while 7.1 says layer 6 and 7.4 drops the layer the email named. (2) Glossary makes the Swiss-cheese model "Anthropic's name"; it is James Reason's safety model. (3) Recap generalises Who&When's 14.2% from "the best automated method" to "automated tools".

findings.checklist_item: Accuracy: contradictions between lessons; Flow: when a lesson says 'layer N', name it
findings.title: Which layer owns 5.5's telemetry: 6.4 says layer 5, 7.1 says layer 6, 7.4 drops the layer the email gave
findings.claim: 6.4 line 553 reads "computed from the traces of 5.5 (the layer-5 traces)". 7.1 line 113 says 5.5's observability "is also part of layer 6", and 1.4 lists tracing under layer 6 (feedback and evals). The PR body says the 7.4 email placed online evals "on layer-5 telemetry" and the notes silently removed the layer. So the course now disagrees with itself, and the new 7.4 resolved the disagreement by omission rather than by a note, which REVIEW.md rule 6 asks for when the email looks wrong.
findings.evidence: weeks/week-06-evaluation-1.md:553 "(the layer-5 traces)"; weeks/week-07-evaluation-2-and-iteration.md:113 "which is also part of layer 6"; weeks/week-01-what-an-agent-is.md 1.4 layer list: "6. Feedback and evals. Tests, linters, type checks, tracing, and the eval suite"; PR description, "Possible errors in the emails".
findings.proposed_change: Change 6.4 line 553 to "(the layer-6 traces from 5.5)" or drop the parenthetical, so 6.4, 7.1 and 7.4 agree with 1.4. In 7.4 "Where it lives", keep the current wording; optionally add one clause: "(the brief put this telemetry in layer 5; 1.4 places tracing in layer 6)". Re-run python3 tools/check_links.py . after editing.

findings.checklist_item: Accuracy: is every claim correct; glossary entries define terms plainly
findings.title: Glossary attributes the Swiss-cheese model to Anthropic; it is James Reason's safety model
findings.claim: The entry says "Anthropic's name for stacking several imperfect evaluation layers". The Swiss cheese model of accident causation is James Reason's (1990), widely used in aviation and healthcare safety; Anthropic's eval guide borrows the term. The lesson body (line 546, "Anthropic's eval guide calls the whole stack a Swiss-cheese model") is accurate; the glossary overstates it.
findings.evidence: glossary.md:934; weeks/week-07-evaluation-2-and-iteration.md:546. James Reason, "Human error: models and management", BMJ 2000;320:768, https://www.bmj.com/content/320/7237/768 (the Swiss cheese model).
findings.proposed_change: Reword: "James Reason's safety-engineering picture, which Anthropic's eval guide applies to monitoring: stack several imperfect evaluation layers, because no single layer catches everything. See 7.4."

findings.checklist_item: Fact preservation: a recap must not generalise or strengthen a claim beyond the lesson body
findings.title: Recap turns Who&When's "best automated method" into "automated tools"
findings.claim: The recap says "Automated tools find it only 14.2% of the time (Who&When)". 7.1 (line 125) and the glossary say the 14.2% is the best automated method's rate on the decisive step in that benchmark. "Automated tools" as a class is a stronger and vaguer claim than the body supports.
findings.evidence: weeks/week-07-evaluation-2-and-iteration.md:125 "the best automated method found the responsible agent 53.5% of the time, but the decisive step only 14.2% of the time" vs line 926.
findings.proposed_change: Reword line 926: "On Who&When, the best automated method found it only 14.2% of the time."

findings.evidence: Lines 435, 729, 789, 877 of the new file; STYLE.md "Plain language", third bullet. Different terms from PR12-F3, same rule.

findings.checklist_item: Accuracy: worked answers answer the exercise as set
findings.title: 7.4 answer (c) describes a step and a gradual slide for the same planted drift
findings.claim: The exercise (line 605) plants a step from night 15: confirmed rate 85% → 60%. The answer first computes z ≈ 3.8 for that step and says the earliest alert is night 18, then adds "A gradual slide shows up in the rolling window around nights 20–22, which is 3–7 nights late". A reader cannot tell whether the answer is 3 nights late (the planted step) or 5–7 nights late (a slide the exercise did not plant).
findings.proposed_change: Make the second case explicit: "If the drop were gradual instead of a step, the rolling window would catch it around nights 20–22, 5–7 nights late." Then "3–7 nights late" covers both cases cleanly.

findings.checklist_item: Accuracy: arithmetic and counts; worked answers answer the exercise as set
findings.title: 7.2 answer scores code 6 as a wrong ticket, but the open code describes a note, not a ticket
findings.claim: The rule at line 321 scores a wrong ticket 3, no ticket 2, a caught or vague failure 1. Category A totals 6, which needs code 6 at 3, and the text says code 6 "gave a false 'normal' verdict". The open code (line 292) is "vendor 429 after 2 stations → note 'weather normal'": a note, with no ticket named. Under the rule as written code 6 is unscored, and if it were 2, A would tie B at 5 and the ranking's top target would be ambiguous.
findings.proposed_change: Either state that code 6 ended in a wrong ticket ("…→ note 'weather normal' → meter ticket filed" at line 292, if that is what the email says), or extend the rule at line 321: "a wrong ticket, or a false 'normal' verdict that closes a hypothesis, is 3". If the email does neither, the author should say which reading it took.
